sections.html:
Monroe County's deeds office takes recordings Monday through Friday between 8:30 a.m. and 4 p.m. A real property document that arrives after 3:00 p.m. is handled on the next working day, so the practical cutoff for same-day posting is an hour earlier than the closing time. Ask the office for its current counter location and e-recording instructions before sending a courier.

Most sellers never visit. Their title agent carries the deed in and pays the charge from the closing funds.

Every instrument, whether a deed, a mortgage or a lis pendens, costs a flat $30 however long it runs. The amount already includes the Michigan remonumentation and automation fees. The county accepts cash, checks and credit cards, and a card adds 3 percent, with a floor of $2.

Monroe County Register of Deeds charges that sellers meet
ServiceFee
Deed or mortgage, any page count$30
Each added instrument assigned or discharged in one document$3 on top of the flat fee
Certifying a recorded document$5
Real estate copy, per page$1
Tax certificate for a warranty deed, up to 5 descriptions$5, then $0.20 per extra description
State tax lien search certificate$1

UCC copies run $2 per page, and a recorded plat copy on letter paper is $1. One exception removes the $3 add-on: a document that moves from the State of Michigan or a local government to a Land Bank Authority.

The state tax is $7.50 per $1,000 and the county tax is $1.10 per $1,000 of total consideration, so $8.60 combined. The county's fee page has the full schedule.

State law makes the seller liable, with payment due at the county treasurer within 15 days after the deed changes hands. MCL 207.526 exempts several kinds of deeds, among them gifts to children and grandchildren, deeds that simply confirm title, and foreclosure transfers. Warranty deeds, master deeds, land contracts and land contract assignments with a covenant of warranty must also show a certificate from the county treasurer's office under MCLA 211.135.

sections.h2: Searching for a deed by name, not address
sections.html:
The office searches by name only and asks for a grantor or grantee plus an approximate year. Staff cannot trace ownership from a street address. A person who lacks the owner's name can get the names on the tax roll from the County Equalization Department or a city assessor, though the roll may list someone other than the true owner.

That rule matters when a relative's house is being sold. Before asking a title company to search, collect these items and have the search check for any lis pendens or lien:

  • The earlier deed or deeds in the family.
  • Probate papers, if an estate owned the house.
  • The exact spelling of every owner's name, with the approximate year of each transfer.

Tax lien searches are priced separately: $1 for a state tax lien certificate and $6 per name for a federal one.

Uniform Commercial Code filings can surface in a title search. A standard form filing and a termination of a filing each cost $30. UCC search information runs only through June 30, 2001, because realty-related filings after July 1, 2001 are recorded in the real estate index alone.

When checking for a lien on a house, search the real estate index, not the personal property files.

sections.h2: Selling a home in Monroe County
sections.html:
Monroe is the only Michigan county touching Lake Erie, and the city of Monroe is both county seat and largest city. The Port of Monroe and the Enrico Fermi nuclear station in Frenchtown Charter Township give the lakeshore an industrial character. Nine public school districts operate within the county, and its district-of-choice policy lets a family enroll in any district with room.

The 2025 estimate is 156,004 people in 67,494 housing units. Owners hold 81.7 percent of homes, and half of owner-occupied houses sit above $228,900. Renters pay a median $1,059.

A legal description matters more here than a street address. The Toledo War settlement of 1836 left the Lost Peninsula in Erie Township separated from the rest of Michigan by the state line, and most of that land is a marina. A 1973 agreement ran the line through tiny Turtle Island in Lake Erie, giving Erie Township the Michigan half.

Lakeshore and river parcels raise their own questions about bottomland and easements. If your house touches Lake Erie, the River Raisin or Sandy Creek, hand the title company your survey and any earlier easements at the start, so the exceptions on the title commitment are known well before the buyer's deadline.

Start a few weeks ahead. Gather the earlier deed, the exact owner names and any survey. Ask the title agent whether the deed needs a treasurer's certificate, and order it before closing. The agent sends the deed in before 3:00 p.m. with the $30 fee and the transfer tax, and the seller owes that tax unless an exemption is stated on the deed.

A cash sale skips lender appraisal, but the recording steps are the same. Check that the deed shows up in the index afterward under the right names.

If the house came to you through an estate, bring the probate papers, because the title agent needs the chain of ownership to line up name by name. If the house was a gift from a parent or grandparent, or the deed only confirms title, mention it early. Those transfers may be exempt from transfer tax, but the exemption has to be stated on the deed itself, so it cannot be added after recording.

Card payments cost extra, so ask the agent whether the closing funds will cover the fee by check. Expect the recorded deed to come back to the buyer or lender, and ask for your own copy for your sale file.

One more practical point: the county will not look up a deed by street address, so when a buyer's agent asks you for the recording details later, keep the owner names and the approximate year of the transfer handy. Those two items are what the office needs to find the document again quickly.

If anything in the paperwork looks unusual, such as a name spelled two ways across old deeds, tell the title agent before closing so it can be fixed with a corrective document rather than discovered at the counter.

faqs.q: What hours does the Monroe County deeds office keep?
faqs.a: Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. Anything real property related that comes in after 3:00 p.m. is recorded or filed the following working day.

faqs.q: How much is the flat charge for a deed in Monroe County?
faqs.a: It is $30 per document regardless of length. Extra instruments assigned or discharged add $3 each, and certifying a copy adds $5. Plain copies of real estate records are $1 a page, and the warranty deed tax certificate is a separate charge.

faqs.q: Does the Monroe County office search by property address?
faqs.a: No. It needs a grantor or grantee name plus an approximate year. The Equalization Department or a city assessor can supply the name on the tax roll.

faqs.q: Which transfer tax rates apply in Monroe County?
faqs.a: $1.10 per $1,000 for the county and $7.50 per $1,000 for the state, based on total consideration. The seller pays unless an exemption is stated on the deed.

faqs.q: How can I pay at the Monroe County counter?
faqs.a: Cash, checks and credit cards are accepted. A card carries a 3 percent fee with a $2 minimum, so a check costs less on a large closing.
